definition: An eigenface ( EYE-gən-) is the name given to a set of eigenvectors when used in the computer vision problem of human face recognition.
details: The approach of using eigenfaces for recognition was developed by Sirovich and Kirby and used by Matthew Turk and Alex Pentland in face classification. The eigenvectors are derived from the covariance matrix of the probability distribution over the high-dimensional vector space of face images. The eigenfaces themselves form a basis set of all images used to construct the covariance matrix. This produces dimension reduction by allowing the smaller set of basis images to represent the original training images. Classification can be achieved by comparing how faces are represented by the basis set.

explainer.lead: Eigenfaces turn a collection of face images into a small set of shared building blocks. Each training face can then be described by how it combines those blocks, making faces easier to represent and compare for recognition.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a box of special face-shaped puzzle pieces that can be mixed in different amounts to rebuild every face in a photo album. Instead of saving every detail of a face, you save its recipe of pieces. To compare two faces, you compare their recipes.
tiers.practitioner: Build the basis from the covariance matrix of the training face-image vectors, then represent each training image using the smaller eigenface basis. Classification compares these basis-based representations, so all compared faces must use the same basis. The basis depends on the images used to construct it; this method supplies the representation, while the classification rule remains a separate choice.
tiers.paperLevel: For face-image vectors drawn from a probability distribution, let C be the covariance matrix; its eigenvectors v satisfy C v = lambda v and are called eigenfaces in this setting. These eigenfaces form a basis for the images used to construct C, allowing lower-dimensional representations whose coordinates can be compared for classification. Sirovich and Kirby developed the recognition approach, and Matthew Turk and Alex Pentland used it in face classification.

explainer.example: Suppose a training set contains photos of several people. After computing the eigenfaces, one person's photo might be represented mostly by basis images 1 and 3, while another person's photo relies more on basis image 2. A classifier compares these compact basis representations instead of directly comparing the full image vectors.

usedIn.name: Human face recognition
usedIn.detail: Uses eigenvector-based face representations to compare and recognize faces.

usedIn.name: Face classification
usedIn.detail: Matthew Turk and Alex Pentland used the approach to classify faces by comparing their basis representations.

explainer.intuition: Rather than treating every pixel as an independent piece of information, eigenfaces find shared patterns across the training faces. A small collection of these patterns can stand in for the original images, giving each face a compact description.
howItWorks: Collect the face images used for training and treat each as a high-dimensional vector.
Form the covariance matrix of the probability distribution over those image vectors.
Take the matrix's eigenvectors as the eigenfaces, forming a basis for the training images.
Represent the original training images with the smaller basis set.
Classify faces by comparing how they are represented by that basis.
explainer.whyItMatters: Eigenfaces reduce the dimension of face-image data while preserving a basis-based representation of the training images. That makes face comparison and classification possible using a smaller description than the original high-dimensional vectors.
misconceptions: An eigenface is not one person's face; it is an eigenvector derived from the training collection.
The basis is not independent of the data: it is formed from the images used to build the covariance matrix.
Eigenfaces provide the representation; classification still requires comparing those representations.
